stories.topic: Turning Down a Fresh Nobel Laureate
stories.summary: When Abhijit Banerjee won the Nobel with Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer, his publishers at Juggernaut offered him for Amit's podcast that same week, but for only one hour. Amit asked for two or three hours and, when they refused, said no. One hour would have meant the standard questions about RCTs. With more time he could have gone back to the 1960s, when Amit's father studied at Presidency College under Abhijit's father, Deepak Banerjee, and traced Abhijit's path through Presidency, JNU and Harvard.
stories.insight: A person is more than the one thing they are famous for, and you only reach that richer story if a conversation has room to wander. The episode also led to Amit's column arguing that Harvard, the cluster, was what made Banerjee.
stories.quote: And that's a kind of conversation I really love to have, where you can get a sense of the soul of a person and not reduce him down to one thing that they're in the public eye for.

stories.topic: The $10 Part That Destroyed a $3.2 Billion Shuttle
stories.summary: Michael Kremer's 1993 paper takes its name from the 1986 Challenger disaster. The space shuttle was a $3.2 billion project, and it exploded because a flimsy $10 O-ring failed. Amit used Kremer's paper in a Times of India column to argue that Harvard, more than Presidency or JNU, was decisive in Banerjee's development.
stories.insight: The lesson is not the cliché that a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. In interdependent work, small differences in quality multiply into huge differences in output, so excellent people need to be surrounded by other excellent people.
stories.quote: it was a $3.2 billion project. And the reason the shuttle exploded was because of a $10 O-ring, you know?

stories.summary: In school and college Oppenheimer was unhappy and didn't fit in anywhere. He even tried to poison his physics teacher with an apple. Then he went to the University of Göttingen, where Max Born, who coined the term 'quantum mechanics', taught him and Dirac and John von Neumann were his classmates.
stories.insight: The same talent can stall in one setting and soar in another. Being among peers of the highest calibre doesn't just teach you, it unlocks you.
stories.quote: He has classmates of the caliber of Dirac and John von Neumann, and he goes to an entirely different level.

stories.topic: A Paper Written Before the Co-Authors Ever Met
stories.summary: Ajay, Ila Patnaik and Achim Zeileis, a statistician in Vienna, got talking on mailing lists and realised they were chasing different pieces of a correlated puzzle. They wrote a paper together that Ajay counts among the nicest of his life, using only email and SVN, with no video calls. They met in person only afterwards.
stories.insight: Internet-scale collaboration can produce serious work. Ajay still argues that remote teams need periodic in-person rapport, because without it humour gets misread and conversation turns robotic.
stories.quote: But we got all the way to our first paper without even video calls, just on email and SVN.

stories.summary: Stuck in a remote corner of Tamil Nadu and cut off from the world's mathematics, Ramanujan did not despair about not being at Cambridge. He set about rebuilding 19th-century mathematics on his own. His breakthrough came when he reached Hardy and connected to the mathematics of the 20th century. Ajay pairs this with the early University of Chicago, whose distance from the East Coast universities fostered independent, unfashionable thinking.
stories.insight: Distance from the cluster is a handicap but not a death sentence. Being away from the mainstream can even breed originality.
stories.quote: Ramanujan started rebuilding the mathematics of the 19th century because he was completely cut off from the mathematics of the world.

stories.topic: Anand Versus the Soviet School of Chess
stories.summary: The Soviet Union made chess a state project. Functionary Nikolai Krylenko called for 'a five-year plan for chess' (Stalin later purged him in 1938). Chess was taught in schools like maths, and a shared body of heuristics was passed down by trainers. Devangshu Datta told Amit that Indian players facing East Europeans in the 1980s felt like self-taught HSC maths kids up against postgrads: 'in the post mortem, the opponent would say, oh, my trainer taught us that with this structure you have to play this way. And you'd be like, shit.' Viswanathan Anand grew up in the Philippines, where a TV chess programme set puzzles; he won so often that they asked him to stop entering and offered him all the chess books he wanted. Without Soviet training, he became world champion.
stories.insight: A system that congregates and trains talent builds a knowledge base that lone geniuses must rebuild from scratch. That makes Anand's achievement staggering, and also makes him an outlier rather than a model.
stories.quote: the metaphor I draw for it is like someone taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and winning the damn thing.

stories.topic: Where Dreams Come to Die and Art Comes to Be Corrupted
stories.summary: On a Seen and the Unseen episode, Vikram Sathaye told Amit about bright kids from small Maharashtra towns who arrive in Bombay steeped in Vijay Tendulkar and local art forms. Surrounded by shallow industry people, and insecure about being called 'vernie', a year later the same kid meets Vikram at a party and says, 'Dude, how are you doing? Let's go chill.'
stories.insight: Clusters don't only lift talent up. Their incentives and status games can also flatten it, and the homogenising pull of the city can strip away what made someone distinctive.
stories.quote: where dreams come to die and art comes to be corrupted.

stories.summary: Vinay Singhal built Stage.in as a 'Netflix for Bharat' that streams content in dialects such as Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and Rajasthani rather than in major languages. VCs told him it would never work. He charged Netflix rates, reached around 300,000 subscribers and raised a big funding round. Vinay described a 'reverse migration from Bollywood': Haryanvi creators who once headed to Bombay are coming home, and a Haryanvi industry of around 3,000 people now exists.
stories.insight: Urbanisation tends to erase dialects and subcultures. Technology and capitalism can now build new congregations that keep them alive.
stories.quote: Vinay described something which he called the reverse migration from Bollywood.

stories.topic: Walking Through a Government in Exile
stories.summary: In McLeod Ganj, Ajay visited the Tibet Museum, which sits inside the complex of the Central Tibetan Administration. The CTA has a Department of Finance, a Department of Home and other tidy structures. It is funded by donations, has no taxation and no coercive power. Ajay is proud that India has sheltered Tibetan refugees even when it was costly, but he wondered whether this 'wannabe state' could become the core of a future Tibetan government.
stories.insight: Play-acting statehood is admirable and poignant, but it isn't training for the real thing. He contrasts it with de Gaulle's Free French in London, who focused only on freeing France rather than on running ministries.
stories.quote: But here you have a living, breathing government in exile.

stories.topic: Warsaw's Communist HQ Becomes the Stock Exchange
stories.summary: In Warsaw, Ajay heard how, after communism ended, Poland took the Communist Party office, the biggest and most powerful building in the city, and turned it into the stock exchange.
stories.insight: Having lived through communism, Eastern Europeans wanted to run as far from it as possible. That intent, combined with EU membership, helped them build capable liberal democracies.
stories.quote: And they turned it into the stock exchange because they were making a statement that we are finished with this stuff and we now want to learn to be a capitalist country.

stories.topic: The IBBI Plan That Was Shelved
stories.summary: When the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India was being set up, MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain led the writing of a project plan to build a high-quality bankruptcy regulator over two years. It was the closest India has come to building a coercive institution with care. In practice the law was notified anyway, and a handful of people were expected to deliver overnight.
stories.insight: India knows how to build regulators properly. It hasn't yet learned to give that work the patience it gives to building a bridge.
stories.quote: In reality, the law was notified and overnight five people were expected to perform.

stories.summary: Before GST, Amit wrote an essay on Gandhi's Dandi Salt March. What surprises people is that the tax on salt was far higher in independent India than it had been under the British Empire, and Amit suspects it still is under GST.
stories.insight: Swapping a foreign ruler for a domestic one doesn't remove the extractive state. Amit sees India's state as a continuation of the colonial one, designed to rule rather than serve.
stories.quote: So that alone tells you that our freedom struggle, such as it is, is deeply incomplete.

recommendations.item: Why Abhijit Banerjee Had to Go Abroad to Achieve Glory
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His Times of India column, written after he turned down a one-hour podcast with the newly minted Nobel laureate.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the episode's core claim: talent congregates, and Harvard was critical to Banerjee's development. It uses Kremer's O-Ring paper as the mechanism.

recommendations.item: The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development
recommendations.creator: Michael Kremer
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a seminal 1993 paper and builds Chapter 1 around it.
recommendations.reason: It explains with simple multiplication why small differences in skill create huge differences in output and pay, and why the best people cluster together.

recommendations.item: The O-Ring Model (Marginal Revolution University video)
recommendations.creator: Tyler Cowen
recommendations.context: Amit admits he may not explain Kremer's model eloquently and points listeners to this video.
recommendations.reason: He calls it fantastic and says it explains the model in detail, better than his own on-air summary.

recommendations.item: My Hero, Oppenheimer (Episode 5 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while telling how Oppenheimer was transformed at Göttingen.
recommendations.reason: Fuller background on Oppenheimer, the episode's prime example of a misfit who flourished once he was among peers of his calibre.

recommendations.item: The Rise of the Creative Class
recommendations.creator: Richard Florida
recommendations.context: Introduced as a theory 'orthogonal' to Kremer's on why talent clusters.
recommendations.reason: It argues that growth follows creative congregation: open, diverse cities draw entrepreneurs, artists and gay and lesbian communities, and capital then chases that talent.

recommendations.item: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His year-end episode with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas, both experienced in the film industry.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of Vikram's story about talented small-town kids losing their depth in Bombay, a reminder that clusters can corrupt as well as uplift.

recommendations.item: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (Episode 291 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His conversation with the founder of Stage.in, recorded about a year before this episode.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of the 'reverse migration from Bollywood' and of how a dialect-first streaming business proved sceptical VCs wrong.

recommendations.creator: Vinay Singhal
recommendations.context: Described as 'Netflix for Bharat', streaming content in dialects such as Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and Rajasthani.
recommendations.reason: A live example of technology and capitalism countering the city's homogenising pull, keeping dialects and local film industries alive.

recommendations.item: The Tamilian Gentleman Who Took on the World
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His ESPN feature on Viswanathan Anand, from which he quotes Devangshu Datta.
recommendations.reason: It shows how big the gap was between self-taught Indian players and Soviet-trained ones, and so how extraordinary Anand's rise was.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His pre-GST essay on Gandhi's Dandi Salt March.
recommendations.reason: It makes the surprising point that independent India taxed salt far more than the British did, evidence that the freedom struggle is incomplete.

recommendations.item: What is the New Chinese Currency Regime?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah, Achim Zeileis and Ila Patnaik
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Ajay's story of collaborating with Zeileis and Patnaik over mailing lists and email.
recommendations.reason: It is Ajay's example of serious research produced by a team spread across countries.

recommendations.context: Prompted by the Tibet Museum T-shirt Ajay was wearing; the museum sits inside the Central Tibetan Administration complex.
recommendations.reason: Unlike many Indian museums it is done well, with artefacts that trigger the mind. Walking the lanes of a living government in exile also makes you think hard about what a state is.

recommendations.item: Building the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
recommendations.creator: MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain
recommendations.context: The project plan for setting up the IBBI over two years.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it a milestone in India's journey: a real plan for building an organisation that will wield coercive power, even though it was largely ignored in practice.

recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Raised when Ajay says India's policy community suffers an intellectual failure on the basics of institution design.
recommendations.reason: The book is built on public choice theory: giving an organisation coercive power can easily go bad, and the fix is checks and balances, not a better CEO.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Amit's pick of the week: Orwell's collected essays, not his novels, in a volume arranged chronologically. Ajay seconds it, saying he wants 'to sell that book to everybody'.
recommendations.reason: It is a chronological look at Orwell the thinker. It is also Amit's cure for writer's block: two or three pieces on any subject and the clarity and rhythm of Orwell's prose 'would free something within me'.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: The essay Amit asked every young writer he edited to read.
recommendations.reason: He calls it 'such a primer on clear writing'.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Amit's Orwell recommendation.
recommendations.reason: A companion piece to Amit's segment on Orwell, clear writing and the link between writing and thinking.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: Amit reads aloud a long passage from this late Orwell book review, tying back to the previous episode's discussion of Gandhi.
recommendations.reason: It shows what a beautiful writer and thinker Orwell was: sceptical of sainthood yet fair, and alert to the shrewd, able person inside Gandhi.

recommendations.creator: Joan Didion
recommendations.context: Quoted during Amit's argument that writing and thinking feed each other; the show notes link to her books.
recommendations.reason: Her line 'I don't know what I think until I write it down' sums up writing as a way of discovering your own thoughts. Amit calls the piece it comes from an amazing essay.

recommendations.item: How Cormac McCarthy Became a Copy-Editor for Scientific Books and One of the Most Influential Articles in Economics
recommendations.creator: Josh Jones
recommendations.context: Ajay's addition to Amit's writing segment, aimed at every STEM researcher.
recommendations.reason: Watching a master of language like Cormac McCarthy clean up a scientific paper is a delight and a lesson in how research should be written.

recommendations.creator: Deirdre McCloskey
recommendations.context: Added as a bonus recommendation; Amit calls McCloskey a great economist and great writer.
recommendations.reason: It teaches how to write about economics, or any complex subject, in clear language for lay readers. That's exactly what his writing students from sociology or anthropology need, since their fields reward jargon as an insider signal.

recommendations.creator: William Easterly
recommendations.context: Ajay's pick of the week, building on the O-Ring discussion of development economics.
recommendations.reason: It's a bit dated but gets the basics right, knocking out the faddish ideas that have damaged development. It leaves you asking what your theory of growth really is, and most development and philanthropy are still gripped by those wrong ideas.

recommendations.creator: William Easterly
recommendations.context: The one Easterly book Amit has read, mentioned after Ajay's pick.
recommendations.reason: A classic on why the West's efforts to aid the rest have done so much ill and so little good, by a fantastic, clear writer and great thinker.

core_ideas.explanation: New technology often borrows the look of the old to put users at ease. Apple's reading app looked like a wooden bookshelf, and sound software shows virtual knobs. Words do the same: we still say 'rolling' with no film cans in sight. Conventions like the QWERTY keyboard stay long after their reason has vanished. Amit thinks there are more harmful versions of this, forms of the past we've outgrown but can't escape. Ajay adds that evolution tuned how fast the mind updates its models, so this stickiness runs deep.
core_ideas.quote: once you've set a particular way of doing something, once you've set a convention, we're kind of stuck there.

core_ideas.explanation: Kremer's insight is that in complex work, quality multiplies rather than adds. In Amit's example, ten people performing at 0.99 produce 9.05; at 0.95, 5.99; at 0.90, just 3.49. A barely visible skill gap becomes a huge output gap, so a 0.99 person can earn two or three times a 0.95 person. The effect is strongest where quality beats quantity (one great novelist beats three mediocre ones) and where a task has thousands of links that must all hold. The result: the best people gain most by clustering with each other.
core_ideas.quote: So a small difference in talent leads to a massive difference in output and productivity.

core_ideas.explanation: Mass manufacturing found another answer to the O-Ring problem: precision standardisation. A car has 10,000 parts, yet it works because every ball bearing is within tight tolerances. Software does the same with APIs, testable black boxes that 'had better just work'. Where interfaces are defined, people can work apart without talking. Filmmaking is the opposite extreme, with fuzzy, personal relationships among hundreds of people, which is why it needs proximity.
core_ideas.quote: Achieve great ladders of complexity when we are guaranteed this plug compatibility.

core_ideas.concept: Contracting Is Harder Than the Work
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay splits creative collaboration into two stages. First comes agreeing who does what, how decisions get made and how resources are shared. Then comes implementation. The first stage needs people who know and trust each other, which is the real magic of hubs like London, New York and Cambridge, Massachusetts. Implementation can then be done remotely, anywhere. Amit adds that meeting online comes with an agenda, while meeting in person allows digressions and banter where new thoughts emerge.
core_ideas.quote: I will suggest that the contracting is a bigger problem than the actual work.

core_ideas.concept: Capital Chases Talent: The Creative Class
core_ideas.explanation: Richard Florida argues that growth follows creative congregation. Open, diverse cities attract entrepreneurs, artists and gay and lesbian communities. Capital follows them, starting a virtuous cycle, or a vicious one where talent leaves. Network effects reinforce it: founders go where the best coders are, and coders go where the startups are. Amit ties this to the 'looking-glass self': we shape ourselves in the reflections of others, so the company we keep shapes who we become.
core_ideas.quote: one consequence of talent coming together is that capital then chases that talent, and then it becomes a virtuous cycle in that particular place

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that Indian middle-class parents overstate how make-or-break clusters are. Books and the internet have changed how people acquire knowledge, and Ramanujan built greatness far from Cambridge. Amit agrees individuals should tell themselves this for morale. But geniuses like Ramanujan and Anand are rare, and many equally gifted people never reached a cluster and stayed invisible. Exceptions inspire; they shouldn't shape policy.
core_ideas.quote: there are countless Ramanujans and Anands who have been lost to us who are unseen

core_ideas.concept: In the Humanities, Authenticity Is King
core_ideas.explanation: In STEM, problems are universal and you can play a global game from anywhere. To understand human societies you have to be inside your subject. Every conversation and scene feeds intuition, so Indian economics is best studied in India. Ajay felt 'a certain emptiness' when abroad and away from his source material. The same logic explains why Hindi films get made in Bombay.
core_ideas.quote: if your thing is the humanities and social sciences, then really authenticity is king.

core_ideas.concept: Brain Drain Is a Question About Home
core_ideas.explanation: Amit reframes the old worry about IIT graduates leaving India. Each of them is making a rational choice and should. The real question is why they have to leave, and what it would take to build centres of excellence here. Right now, he argues, India is chasing good people away, and those who stay do so despite the odds. Policymakers should create the conditions for talent to congregate.
core_ideas.quote: The question then is that why are they having to go abroad? What can we do to create centers of excellence here so that people feel inspired, people feel happy?

core_ideas.explanation: Inside India, engineers stream from the Hindi heartland to hubs like Bangalore, Pune, Hyderabad and Madras. Ajay notes a remarkable claim he has heard: the US has the world's best engineering workforce and India is now second. The top end of a distribution multiplied by 1.4 billion people produces real critical mass.
core_ideas.quote: if you want a cute 20-man team, you're okay in Finland. But if you want 2,000 people, you'll come to India because the depth of the bench is phenomenal.

core_ideas.explanation: Urbanisation is the engine of human progress, but it pressures newcomers to conform. A Bhojpuri or Maithili speaker who moves to a Hindi-speaking city often drops their dialect so as not to seem 'vernie'. Technology and capitalism can now build virtual congregations, like Stage.in's dialect content, that keep subcultures alive. They can't fully replace in-person meeting, though.
core_ideas.quote: one of the side effects is that homogenization happens, you can lose dialects, you can lose subcultures.

core_ideas.explanation: You don't need a Bollywood-sized agglomeration, but some projects can't happen below a threshold: a movie needs a team of at least 10 to 20. Bhopal may lack an engineering culture while Pune has one. Ajay takes the middle road: agglomerations matter and we need each other, but Silicon Valley isn't the only place where ideas can flourish.
core_ideas.quote: So there is a minimum economy of scale, at which point things can take off.

core_ideas.concept: Sturgeon's Law Versus Incentives for Mediocrity
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay counters Amit's critique of Bollywood: 99% of everything is crass and shallow, including Indian and Silicon Valley startups. Amit sharpens his point. The issue isn't that most output is bad. It's that a cluster's incentives can push a genuinely good person into producing bad work.
core_ideas.quote: My point was that a good person who can do great work will come to Bollywood and produce crap because there are incentives for mediocrity.

core_ideas.explanation: The Central Tibetan Administration has the trappings of a state but runs on donations, so it is fundamentally a nice organisation. Ajay argues that no amount of play-acting prepares you for the poison of coercive power. It may even backfire through 'isomorphic mimicry', lulling people into thinking that departments with the right names mean they are ready to govern.
core_ideas.quote: You don't develop state capability without actually fighting with the battle of the evil that is coercive power.

core_ideas.concept: Violent Freedom Struggles Breed Bad States
core_ideas.explanation: Most post-colonial states fared badly, and worst where freedom came through armed struggle. Once unleashed, violence doesn't go away. It changes people and lifts the wrong kind of person to the top, when a decent state needs something like a philosopher king. Gandhi's ahimsa was the 'one simple piece of magic' India got right at the outset.
core_ideas.quote: violent movements bubble up successful military generals who are rarely philosopher kings.

core_ideas.concept: Why Eastern Europe Succeeded and Russia Failed
core_ideas.explanation: East Germany inherited West Germany's whole institutional package overnight and flourished, though like north versus south Italy, the regional gap persists. The rest of Eastern Europe and the Baltics built institutions from scratch. They wanted to flee communism, and the EU's 20,000 pages of draft laws and treaties kept them from certain mistakes, with Hungary and Poland the laggards. Russia privatised and created markets overnight, with Jeff Sachs among those pushing, but neglected the state. Liberal democracy means constitutionalism, rule of law and checks and balances, not just elections every five years.
core_ideas.quote: You need the state, you need liberal democracy, you need freedom, and freedom is coded into laws and state institutions.

core_ideas.explanation: India accepts that a bridge takes years of project management before the ribbon-cutting. A new regulator like a food safety authority should be treated the same way. It needs organisational design, written processes, staff trained to work within them, IT systems and repeated review of checks and balances. Powers should then be notified in stages, starting with trivial transactions. Launching a coercive agency overnight sends it into permanent firefighting, invites lobbying for favours and attracts the wrong leaders.
core_ideas.quote: But nobody expects a zero day lag between the decision to have a bridge and the bridge.

core_ideas.concept: An Institution's DNA Lives in Its Law
core_ideas.explanation: Amit asks whether all institutions inevitably decay. Ajay says no. Laws either create arbitrary power or create checks and balances. Coercive power is like a nuclear reactor and needs enough 'cladding' around it, after which experience can feed back into steady improvement. Indian laws mostly assume people are good and recklessly confer discretion. Both hosts agree on the goal: a system where even the worst person in power can't do much harm.
core_ideas.quote: Most of our Indian laws are based on an optimistic reading of human beings.

core_ideas.explanation: When an Indian agency malfunctions, the reflex is to demand a better CEO. Ajay calls this primitive. The real debate, grounded in public choice theory, is about the right checks and balances for each organisation. Amit is gloomier: he sees India's state as designed to rule rather than serve, a continuation of the colonial state that is mighty hard to change.
core_ideas.quote: Mostly in India today, we are at the more primitive level of a great man theory that we see a malfunctioning organization and we want a better CEO.

core_ideas.explanation: A century ago, India's chattering classes argued about what free India would look like. They got the state wrong, assuming it would be led by good people like Gandhi and Nehru, when coercive power attracts the most venal. Ajay sees today as a research and development phase: build the knowledge and community now, so that when the public demands to know why some agency is failing, the answers are ready.
core_ideas.quote: So we are in that R&D phase of figuring out what a successful, prosperous India would look like.

core_ideas.explanation: Clear thinkers tend to write clearly, but the reverse matters just as much. Forcing yourself to write clearly exposes holes in your argument and gaps in your knowledge, and can change your mind. Didion said she didn't know what she thought until she wrote it down. Amit paraphrases McCloskey's view that writing is research, not something that follows it. Obscure prose is usually a sign of muddled thinking or insider signalling.
core_ideas.quote: if you force yourself to write clearly, you are forced to think better because you cannot hide behind, you know, abstract words or vague jargon

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay, explaining that some work needs a minimum team size, offers 'trivial production projects like some YouTube podcast with an eclectic name, everything is everything' as what you can make with essentially no team.
Amit scolds Ajay for hurting their producer Vartika's feelings with talk of tiny teams. Ajay protests: 'it's a three-man team and you know we couldn't have made a movie even if we wanted.'
On how much time he needs with a guest: Amit asked for two or three hours with Banerjee, 'and today of course I would insist on five hours or nothing.'
Amit notes that Orwell, like Bastiat, died at 49, 'which is my age right now. So may I somehow reach the end of December, I'll be very happy.'

Young Anand kept winning the puzzle contests on a Philippine TV chess show until, as Amit remembers it, they called and said: 'Look, you're winning everything, just stop entering, we'll give you all the chess books you want once and for all.'
Devangshu Datta on facing Soviet-trained players: the opponent would explain in the post-mortem that his trainer taught him how to play that structure, 'and you'd be like, shit.'
Amit's images for Anand's feat: 'like someone taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and winning the damn thing', or 'winning Wimbledon today with a wooden racket.'
Amit's test for academic prose: 'whenever I read something full of obfuscatory language, I know that person is full of shit.'
Ajay turns Orwell's dictum into 'Podcasts should be like a windowpane.' Amit explains the source: Orwell's line that good prose should be like a windowpane.
Ajay: Orwell matters more 'now that we know that history did not end', a nod to the 'end of history' idea. Amit: 'And now that nineteen eighty four is approaching.'

Ajay recalls Jerry Pournelle's The Mote in God's Eye, where genetic engineering has given everyone perfect vision, yet people still use the phrase '20/20'. Like the producer still saying 'rolling' with no film cans.

Skeuomorphic design: Apple's early reading app drawn as a physical bookshelf, and knobs on sound-mixing software. Ajay wonders whether Steve Jobs' pinch-on-screen gesture will survive a hundred years.
Freddy, the plush toy on the table, is named after Amit's hero Frédéric Bastiat and after Friedrich Hayek: 'two Freddies, he carries both of them within him.'

Soviet functionary Nikolai Krylenko: 'We must finish once and for all with the neutrality of chess... We must organize shock brigades of chess players and begin immediate realization of a five-year plan for chess.' Stalin purged him in 1938.
'As every Russian schoolboy knows': Ajay's chess-world inside joke for things that seem deep to outsiders but are common knowledge to Soviet-trained kids. The phrase has spread far beyond chess.
The Fischer–Spassky match, which Amit calls seminal because an American genius broke the Soviet dominance of chess.
Charles de Gaulle's French government in exile in London during WWII. Ajay doubts it set up a department of health; it focused on one thing, getting to a free France.
Sturgeon's Law, cited by Amit as 'ninety-eight percent of everything is crap'. Ajay's version: '99% of everything is crass, shallow bullshit', whether Bollywood, Indian startups or Silicon Valley.
'Vernie', the urban Indian put-down for vernacular speakers that pushes small-town talent to drop dialects. Amit says the vernacular is something to celebrate.

Orwell lines recited from memory by Ajay, describing the mood of the 1930s: 'It is forbidden to dream again; we maim our hopes or hide them. The horses are made of chromium steel, and little fat men shall ride them.' Amit's reaction: 'Insane memory.'

From Orwell's 'Reflections on Gandhi', read by Amit: 'Saints should always be judged guilty until they are proved innocent', and that inside the saint 'there was a very shrewd, able person who could, if he had chosen, have been a brilliant success as a lawyer, an administrator, or perhaps even a businessman.'
